categories.name: From the woods
categories.description: Notes from the cabins, the trails and the woodshed.

posts.title: Stacking wood for October
posts.excerpt: Why the cedar goes at the back of the porch stack and the beech at the front.
posts.content:
By the second week of October the porches begin to fill. Ruben splits the cedar in the summer, when it dries fastest, and the beech in the spring, when it is still easy to work. Each cabin gets a stack of roughly two baskets against its north wall, with the cedar at the back for kindling and the beech at the front for the long burn.

Every morning at ten the firewood round reaches every porch. Guests rarely see it happen: a basket appears, the old one is taken, and the stack is squared off again. It is the quietest job in the village and the one people mention most in the visitor book.

If you are arriving in October, bring a warm layer for the evenings and leave the stove to the first basket. A cabin heated slowly with beech feels very different from one heated quickly with cedar, and we are happy to show you how.

posts.title: Why Friday check-in starts at three
posts.excerpt: Behind the scenes of our Friday turnover, four quiet hours between check-out and check-in ensure every cabin is turned, stocked with dry firewood, and aired for the weekend.
posts.content:
At eleven o'clock on a Friday morning, the woodshed office bell rings to mark the departure of our midweek guests. The gravel lane under the beeches falls quiet for a moment as cars head out toward Hollin Vale. For the next four hours, between eleven o'clock check-out and fifteen o'clock check-in, our thirty-eight hectares of mixed cedar and beech woodland become a hive of focused, methodical care. Guests often ask why we do not allow earlier arrivals on a Friday afternoon. The answer lies in the unhurried standard of preparation required to turn twelve whole cabins into silent, welcoming forest sanctuaries.

Sofia Navarro, who leads our housekeeping team, begins her rounds immediately at eleven o'clock. Twelve cabins spread across four distinct sizes mean twelve unique interiors to inspect, air, and clean. Sofia and her assistants move quietly from Fern to Hollow, throwing open the timber windows to let the cool forest air circulate through the bedrooms. Every set of bed linen and cotton towels is stripped and replaced with fresh, pressed bedding. The rain showers are scrubbed, the timber floors are swept, and the induction hobs and ovens are thoroughly cleaned. In each kitchen, crockery, cutlery, kettles, and coffee presses are counted and inspected to match the exact guest count, ensuring everything is in place for self-catering meals.

While housekeeping works inside, co-founder Ruben Okafor and carpenter Tobias Klein attend to the structural and heating needs of each cabin. Every wood stove must be cold-cleaned, with ashes cleared from the firebox and the flue inspected. Tobias checks the porch balustrades and timber latches, ensuring that every window opens smoothly and every timber chair is sturdy. Meanwhile, Ruben loads the handcart at the woodshed workshop to make the firewood round. Every porch receives a freshly split, brim-full basket of seasoned beech and cedar logs, along with dry kindling and fire starters. When autumn winds bring dampness to the clearing, having dry firewood neatly stacked against the porch wall before guests arrive is not merely a courtesy; it is the cornerstone of comfort in the woods.

Down at the woodshed office, booking manager Amira Haddad and weekend host Nora Adeyemi prepare the arrival files. Keys on hand-carved wooden tags are laid out in order along the counter, paired with printed forest trail maps and cabin guides. If guests have arranged to bring a dog to Fern or Beech, clean water bowls and blankets are set in place. If an arrival is scheduled after nineteen o'clock, Amira sets up the private key box codes and verifies that exterior porch lights will switch on automatically at dusk. Forest guide Jonah Pereira stops by after clearing fallen branches from the Short Loop, checking that the four-hundred-metre gravel approach road is clear of obstructions.

By fourteen-thirty, the village has returned to stillness. Co-founder Ilse Marten walks the path between the cabins for a final walkthrough, checking that windows are fastened, hearths are reset, and the scent of fresh cedar and clean timber fills each room. At fifteen o'clock, the woodshed office doors open wide. When the first estate car rolls slowly down the gravel lane from Larch Gate, the cabin is ready, the kindling is laid, and the weekend begins without haste.

posts.title: The beech that fell in March
posts.excerpt: A storm brought down a hundred-year-old beech beside the River path. This is what we did with it.
posts.content:
In the last week of March a storm brought down a beech that had stood beside the River path for more than a century. It missed the nearest cabin by a few metres and left a clearing the size of a small field.

Jonah closed the path for two days while Ruben and Tobias cut the trunk into lengths. The straight sections went to the carpentry shed, where they will become benches for the porches. The rest was split and stacked, and it will heat the stoves this coming winter.

The clearing is already filling with light and, by June, with ferns. The walk is open again, and the stump is the best seat on the river path.
